question: Below about 0.3 K, liquid helium-3 is squeezed until part of it freezes. What happens to its temperature?
options: It rises, as freezing releases heat
It falls, as freezing absorbs heat
answer: It falls. Freezing usually releases heat because the solid is tidier than the liquid. In cold helium-3 it is reversed: quantum rules hold the liquid in near-order, while in the solid each nucleus's spin points any which way. So freezing draws heat in. Cornell physicists squeezed their way to about 2 thousandths of a kelvin.
move: When a rule rests on which side is tidier, check which side is.
trap: Expecting heat to be released, as when water turns to ice.
reference: Richardson, The Pomeranchuk effect, Reviews of Modern Physics, 1997
